%% The abstract is a short summary of the work to be presented in the
%% article.
\begin{abstract}
Multi-agent coordination in heterogeneous manufacturing systems integrating mobile and stationary agents faces fundamental challenges: 
coupled discrete-continuous optimization is computationally intractable, existing 
approaches sacrifice optimality by solving subproblems independently. 
We propose the Hybrid Dynamic Programming (HDP) framework for solving the 
Coupled Discrete-Continuous Heterogeneous Agent Scheduling (CDHAS) problem in 
intelligent manufacturing. HDP decomposes the intractable joint problem into 
Continuous State Space (CSS) trajectory optimization and Discrete Event System 
(DES) task scheduling, coordinating them through iterative refinement with 
proven convergence guarantees. We establish theoretical results on geometric convergence (the iterative 
coordination converges in 6 iterations on average, with empirical 
convergence rate $\rho_{\text{eff}} \approx 0.41$---faster than the 
theoretical worst-case prediction of $0.45$--$0.68$, owing to sparse 
coupling and schedule stability in practice), near-optimality (within 
1.2\% of global optimal), and polynomial \textit{task} complexity 
($O(M^{1.8})$ for fixed agent numbers, where $M$ is the number of tasks, compared to MILP's 
exponential $O(2^M)$). Experiments on a heterogeneous manufacturing system across three problem 
scales (12-60 tasks, with 10 instances per dataset) demonstrate 15--23\%
makespan reduction and 25\% utilization improvement compared to baseline methods, with polynomial \textit{task 
scalability} enabling 100 task problems to be solved in under 2 minutes.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:Chapter_I}

The deployment of intelligent manufacturing systems promises to revolutionize 
industrial production through the coordinated operation of heterogeneous agents. 
These systems integrate mobile agents—such as Automated Guided Vehicles (AGVs) 
navigating factory floors with continuous spatiotemporal dynamics—and stationary 
agents—such as robotic manipulators executing discrete event-driven processing 
tasks~\cite{chryssolouris2023artificial}. While these subsystems 
are often studied independently, their real-world interactions form a 
\textit{Continuous–Discrete Hybrid Agent System (CDHAS)}, where mobile and 
stationary agents exhibit \textit{bidirectional spatiotemporal coupling}—mobile 
agent trajectories constrain discrete task assignments, while task schedules 
constrain mobile agent destinations and arrival times. This coupling requires 
joint optimization of spatial trajectories and discrete task logic to achieve 
efficient production~\cite{giordani2013distributed}.

Such coordination is critical across manufacturing applications. In warehouse 
logistics, AGVs must deliver materials to robotic assembly stations at precise 
times to minimize idle time~\cite{ellithy2024agv}.
This type of applications share a common structure: continuous mobile agents with 
spatiotemporal dynamics must coordinate with discrete stationary agents executing 
event-driven tasks.

However, a fundamental challenge impedes practical deployment: the 
\textit{bidirectional spatiotemporal coupling} between continuous and discrete 
subsystems~\cite{senkul2002logical}. As illustrated in 
Fig.~\ref{fig:intro_problem}, this coupling creates a circular dependency that 
traditional sequential methods cannot resolve effectively.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
    \includegraphics[width=0.85\columnwidth]{fig/fig_intro_problem_new.pdf}
    \Description{Illustration of the introductory problem setup: AGVs and robotic arms.}
\caption{The bidirectional coupling challenge in CDHAS.
\textbf{(a) Physical scenario}: AGV1 starts near RA1 (2m), but RA1 is busy
for 12s; RA2 is idle but 5m away. The spatially greedy choice ignores temporal availability.
\textbf{(b) Circular dependency}: CSS agents require a DES schedule to plan
trajectories, while DES agents require CSS arrival times to schedule tasks---
neither subsystem can be solved independently, and traditional sequential
methods inevitably break this coupling.
\textbf{(c) Consequence}: Greedy-Single assigns AGV1 to the nearest RA1,
creating a 10s idle gap, illustrating the cost of ignoring bidirectional coupling.}
\label{fig:intro_problem}
\end{figure}

Fig.~\ref{fig:intro_problem}(b) illustrates the core challenge: CSS and DES 
are mutually dependent. CSS trajectories constrain which discrete tasks can be 
assigned, while discrete task assignments constrain where CSS agents must travel. 
This creates a circular dependency---neither subsystem can be solved 
independently. As shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:intro_problem}(a), consider a concrete 
scenario where AGV1 starts near RA1 (2\,m away), but RA1 is busy for 12\,s, 
while RA2 is idle but located 5\,m away. Traditional sequential methods that 
optimize subsystems separately break this coupling: as shown in 
Fig.~\ref{fig:intro_problem}(c), Greedy-Single assigns AGV1 to the spatially 
nearest RA1, creating a 10\,s idle gap and a makespan of 18\,s---a direct 
consequence of ignoring the bidirectional spatiotemporal coupling.

Our Hybrid Dynamic Programming (HDP) framework addresses this through a 
\textit{decompose-coordinate-converge} strategy. HDP decomposes the coupled 
problem into Continuous State Space Dynamic Programming (CSS-DP) for trajectory 
optimization and Discrete Event System Dynamic Programming (DES-DP) for task 
scheduling. Solutions are coordinated through iterative refinement that preserves 
coupling constraints while converging to near-optimal joint solutions.

To illustrate why traditional methods fail and how HDP resolves the challenge,
consider the concrete scenario in Fig.~\ref{fig:motivating_example}.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.92\columnwidth]{fig/fig_intro_solution.pdf}
\Description{Illustrative solution snapshot showing AGV routing and task assignment.}
\caption{HDP framework: \textbf{decompose--coordinate--converge} strategy.
\textbf{(a) Physical scenario}: AGV1 starts near RA1 (2m, busy 12s) and RA2
(5m, idle).
\textbf{(b) Decompose}: CSS-DP independently computes that AGV1 reaches RA2
in 5s; DES-DP independently identifies RA2 as immediately available---each
subproblem is tractable in isolation.
\textbf{(c) Coordinate}: CSS-DP and DES-DP iteratively exchange coupling
variables (arrival times $\boldsymbol{\tau}$ and schedule $\mathbf{S}$) via
the Coordinator; makespan decreases geometrically.
\textbf{(d) Converge}: Upon convergence, HDP assigns AGV1 to RA2, trading 3s
extra travel for eliminating a 10s idle gap.}
\label{fig:motivating_example}
\end{figure}

Traditional greedy methods assign AGV1 to RA1 based solely on spatial proximity,
ignoring temporal constraints. This creates a 10-second idle gap where AGV1
waits at RA1 while RA2 remains idle with no material with significant resource underutilization.

In contrast, HDP resolves this through three coordinated steps
(Fig.~\ref{fig:motivating_example}b--d). First, \textit{Decompose}
(Fig.~\ref{fig:motivating_example}b): the coupled problem is split into two
tractable subproblems---CSS-DP independently computes that AGV1 can reach RA2
in 5\,s, while DES-DP independently identifies RA2 as immediately available.
Second, \textit{Coordinate} (Fig.~\ref{fig:motivating_example}c): CSS-DP and
DES-DP iteratively exchange coupling variables---arrival times
$\boldsymbol{\tau}$ from CSS-DP to DES-DP, and updated schedules $\mathbf{S}$
from DES-DP back to CSS-DP---until the solutions are mutually consistent.
Third, \textit{Converge} (Fig.~\ref{fig:motivating_example}d): upon
convergence, HDP assigns AGV1 to RA2 instead. Although AGV1 travels 3\,s
longer (5\,s vs.\ 2\,s), it eliminates the 10-second wait, reducing makespan and get improvement with zero idle gaps.

This example demonstrates the fundamental limitation of sequential optimization:
spatial proximity does not guarantee temporal efficiency.

Beyond the circular dependency, three challenges complicate CDHAS scheduling.
First, \textit{computational intractability}: the coupled continuous-discrete
state space grows exponentially, making direct optimization infeasible~\cite{belotti2013mixed}.
Traditional mixed-integer nonlinear programming (MINLP) approaches suffer from
exponential complexity~\cite{kimiaei2025machine}.
Second, \textit{performance robustness}: real-world manufacturing tasks are
subject to inherent uncertainties such as variations in material properties,
robot performance, and processing conditions, which cause task durations to
deviate from nominal values~\cite{calvaresi2021real}.
Third, \textit{limited generalizability}: existing methods are often tailored
to fixed configurations and fail to maintain consistent performance across
varying task volumes, agent counts, or workspace
layouts~\cite{mahajan2022generalization}.

We make three key contributions:

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*]
    
\item \textbf{Unified modeling and decomposition framework:} We formulate
CDHAS scheduling as coupled optimization over CSS and DES dynamics, introducing
a spatiotemporal logic framework for modeling bidirectional spatiotemporal 
coupling constraints. Exploiting the weak coupling structure of the problem, 
we develop a decomposition into Continuous State Space Dynamic Programming 
(CSS-DP) for trajectory optimization and Discrete Event System Dynamic 
Programming (DES-DP) for task scheduling, coordinated through iterative 
refinement with proven convergence guarantees.
    
\item \textbf{Convergence-guaranteed algorithms with task-scalable implementation:} 
    We develop specialized DP algorithms for each subproblem and an iterative 
    coordination mechanism, prove convergence to coordinately optimal solutions 
    and provide convergence rate analysis. Although the worst-case complexity is polynomial in the number of tasks, agents, and discretization parameters, three practical techniques—reachability-based pruning, adaptive discretization, and warm-start initialization—compress each dominant factor, 
	achieving empirical task complexity $O(M^{1.8})$ for fixed agent numbers and scaling to 100+ task problems within 2 minutes.

\item \textbf{Comprehensive validation:} Experiments on three problem scales
(DS1: 12 tasks, DS2: 30 tasks, DS3: 60 tasks) with 10 random instances per dataset demonstrate  15-23\% makespan reduction and 25\% improvement in CSS agent utilization—a proxy for overall system coordination efficiency—versus traditional methods.
\end{enumerate}

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section~\ref{sec:Chapter_II} 
reviews related work. Section~\ref{sec:Chapter_III} presents the problem 
formulation. Section~\ref{sec:Chapter_IV} 
details the HDP framework, algorithms, and theoretical analysis. 
Section~\ref{sec:Chapter_V} reports experimental results. 
Section~\ref{sec:Chapter_VI} discusses limitations and future directions.

\textbf{Notation:} We use bold lowercase for vectors ($\mathbf{x}$), bold 
uppercase for matrices ($\mathbf{A}$), calligraphic for sets and spaces ($\mathcal{X}$), 
and blackboard bold for standard number sets ($\mathbb{R}$). The notation $[n]$ 
denotes $\{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$, $\|\cdot\|$ denotes Euclidean norm, and 
$|\cdot|$ denotes set cardinality. We use $\mathcal{A}^c = \{A_1^c, \ldots, A_{N_c}^c\}$ 
for CSS agents (mobile robots) and $\mathcal{A}^d = \{A_1^d, \ldots, A_{N_d}^d\}$ 
for DES agents (stationary machines), with $i$ and $j$ used interchangeably 
for $A_i^c$ and $A_j^d$ when context is clear.


\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:Chapter_II}

The scheduling of Continuous--Discrete Hybrid Agent Systems (CDHAS) intersects
three research domains: continuous spatiotemporal system scheduling, discrete
event system scheduling, and hybrid system optimization. While significant
progress has been made in each domain independently, existing approaches have
not adequately addressed the spatiotemporal coupling constraints that arise
when heterogeneous agents with fundamentally different dynamics must operate
in a tightly coordinated manner.


\textbf{Continuous spatiotemporal system scheduling.} Existing methods optimize 
mobile agent trajectories (AGVs, AMRs, drones)~\cite{lian2022spatio}, 
using network flow models~\cite{chen2020yard}, conflict-based search~\cite{cao2025conflict}, 
and dynamic window approaches~\cite{liu2019route}. These methods are designed for 
purely continuous agent systems, focusing on trajectory feasibility and efficiency 
such as collision avoidance and travel time minimization~\cite{lei2025cooperative, zheng2024continuous}. 
However, they do not address the joint scheduling of heterogeneous agents with 
fundamentally different dynamics.

\textbf{Discrete event system scheduling.} Discrete event scheduling has been 
extensively studied in manufacturing systems, focusing on job-shop scheduling, 
flexible manufacturing, and robotic task sequencing~\cite{wang2024smart}. Luo et al.\ \cite{luo2016using} introduced Scheduling 
Metric Temporal Logic (SMTL) for complex scheduling with temporal constraints. 
Zhou et al.\ \cite{zhou2016timed} utilized Metric Interval Temporal Logic 
(MITL) and timed automata for robotic manipulator sequencing. Zheng et al.\ 
\cite{zheng2007temporal} proposed Extended Temporal Logic-based Workflow 
Specification (ETLWS) for grid computing. These methods provide powerful 
tools for modeling operation sequences under temporal and logical constraints~\cite{zhang2024generation}. 
However, they abstract away the continuous physical space in which mobile 
agents operate, treating material delivery as instantaneous or externally 
handled~\cite{pooch2024discrete}.

\textbf{Hybrid system optimization.} Hybrid system research addresses systems
with both continuous dynamics and discrete event behavior using hybrid automata,
mixed-integer programming, and hybrid dynamic programming~\cite{lin2022hybrid}.
Representative approaches include Lipschitz dynamic programming for power grid
scheduling~\cite{shen2022coordinated}, route-reduction-based DP for satellite
scheduling~\cite{liu2019route}, and Coordinated Robust Reserve Scheduling using
ADMM for transmission-distribution networks~\cite{chen2020fully}. While these
methods have made important contributions to continuous-discrete optimization,
they are predominantly designed for domain-specific applications (power systems,
satellite networks) where the coupling is primarily \textit{temporal} (e.g.,
power dispatch timing) rather than \textit{spatiotemporal} (e.g., physical
co-location of mobile agents and processing units). They do not address the
unique challenge of spatiotemporal coupling in multi-agent systems---where
continuous mobile agents must synchronize physical positions and arrival times
with discrete state transitions of processing units.

In the robotics domain, hybrid system optimization is instantiated as
Task and Motion Planning (TAMP)~\cite{zhao2024survey}, a framework that
integrates symbolic task planning with geometric motion planning for systems
where discrete actions (e.g., pick, place, navigate) must be grounded in
continuous motion trajectories. Representative TAMP approaches include:
PDDLStream~\cite{garrett2021integrated}, which combines PDDL-based symbolic planning with sampling-based motion planning;
Logic-Geometric Programming~\cite{driess2021learning}, which formulates TAMP as constrained optimization with logic predicates;
and Asymov~\cite{dantam2016incremental}, which uses SMT solvers for symbolic planning and trajectory optimization.
While these methods advance discrete-continuous integration
for manipulation tasks, they share a structural limitation with respect to
CDHAS: existing TAMP solvers are designed for \textit{feasibility-driven}
planning---finding any valid plan via symbolic search with geometric
feasibility checks---whereas CDHAS requires \textit{optimality-driven}
planning in which AGV arrival times are continuous optimization variables
that directly determine makespan.
Furthermore, CDHAS involves \textit{bidirectional} spatiotemporal
coupling---AGV trajectories constrain Robot Arm schedules and vice versa---which
cannot be resolved by existing TAMP implementations.

Our work fills this gap by: (1) proposing a unified modeling framework that 
integrates \textit{spatiotemporal coupling constraints} (Eq.~\ref{eq:coupling_constraints}) 
with continuous dynamics (Eq.~\ref{eq:css_dynamics}) and discrete event logic 
(Eq.~\ref{eq:precedence}); (2) developing hybrid dynamic programming that 
jointly optimizes task allocation, trajectory planning, and operation sequencing 
under bidirectional spatiotemporal coupling; (3) proving convergence guarantees 
(Theorem~\ref{thm:convergence}) and near-optimality bounds 
(Theorem~\ref{thm:near_optimality}).

\section{Problem Formulation}
\label{sec:Chapter_III}

This section formulates the Coupled Discrete-Continuous Heterogeneous Agent 
Scheduling (CDHAS) problem, integrating continuous spatiotemporal dynamics 
of mobile agents with discrete event logic of stationary agents.

\subsection{System Model}

A CDHAS consists of two types of agents operating in a shared workspace 
$\mathcal{W} \subset \mathbb{R}^2$:

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*, itemsep=3pt]
    \item \textbf{Continuous State Space (CSS) agents} $\mathcal{A}^c = \{A_1^c, \ldots, A_{N_c}^c\}$: 
    Mobile agents (e.g., AGVs) that navigate the workspace with continuous 
    dynamics. Each CSS agent $i$ has state $\mathbf{x}_i^c(t) = [\mathbf{p}_i(t), \mathbf{v}_i(t)]^\top$, 
    where $\mathbf{p}_i(t) \in \mathcal{W}$ is position and $\mathbf{v}_i(t) \in \mathbb{R}^2$ 
    is velocity at time $t$.
    
    \item \textbf{Discrete Event System (DES) agents} $\mathcal{A}^d = \{A_1^d, \ldots, A_{N_d}^d\}$: 
    Stationary agents (e.g., robotic arms) that execute discrete tasks. Each 
    DES agent $j$ is located at fixed position $\mathbf{p}_j^{\text{target}} \in \mathcal{W}$ 
    with discrete state $q_j^d(t) \in \{\text{idle}, \text{processing}, \text{waiting}\}$ 
    and task queue $\mathcal{T}_j = \{T_j^1, \ldots, T_j^{m_j}\}$.
\end{itemize}

The workspace contains static obstacles $\mathcal{O} = \{O_1, \ldots, O_{N_o}\}$ 
that CSS agents must avoid. The planning horizon is $[0, T_{\text{horizon}}]$.

\subsection{Mathematical Model}

\subsubsection{Continuous State Space (CSS) Dynamics}

CSS agents follow kinematic motion models with velocity control:

\begin{equation}
\dot{\mathbf{x}}_i^c(t) = \frac{d\mathbf{x}_i^c}{dt} = 
\begin{bmatrix}
\dot{\mathbf{p}}_i(t) \\
\dot{\mathbf{v}}_i(t)
\end{bmatrix}
= 
\begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf{v}_i(t) \\
\mathbf{u}_i^c(t)
\end{bmatrix}, \quad i \in [N_c]
\label{eq:css_dynamics}
\end{equation}

where $\dot{\mathbf{x}}_i^c(t) = \frac{d\mathbf{x}_i^c}{dt}$ denotes the time 
derivative, $\mathbf{v}_i(t)$ is velocity, and $\mathbf{u}_i^c(t) \in \mathbb{R}^2$ 
is control input (acceleration) subject to:

\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\|\mathbf{v}_i(t)\| &\leq v_{\max}, \quad
\|\mathbf{u}_i^c(t)\| \leq a_{\max}, \\
\mathbf{p}_i(t) &\in \mathcal{W} \setminus \mathcal{O}, \quad
\|\mathbf{p}_i(t) - \mathbf{p}_{i'}(t)\| \geq d_{\text{safe}}, \; \forall i' \neq i
\end{aligned}
\label{eq:css_constraints}
\end{equation}

where $v_{\max}$ is maximum velocity, $a_{\max}$ is maximum acceleration, 
and $d_{\text{safe}}$ is minimum safe distance for collision avoidance.

\subsubsection{Discrete Event System (DES) Logic}

Each task $T_j^k$ represents the processing operation (e.g., welding,
assembly, or inspection) that DES agent $j$ performs on a workpiece
delivered by a CSS agent. The processing duration $d_j^k$ captures
only the arm's active execution time and excludes AGV travel time;
the latter instead determines the earliest feasible scheduled start
time $\tau_j^k$, as formalized by the coupling constraints in
Section~\ref{sec:coupling_cons}.

Tasks are subject to precedence constraints:

\begin{equation}
    T_j^k \prec T_j^{k'} \implies \tau_j^k + d_j^k \leq \tau_j^{k'}, \quad k < k'
    \label{eq:precedence}
\end{equation}

Each DES agent processes at most one task at a time (non-preemptive):

\begin{equation}
    [\tau_j^k,\, \tau_j^k + d_j^k] \cap [\tau_j^{k'},\, \tau_j^{k'} + d_j^{k'}] = \emptyset, \quad k \neq k'
    \label{eq:nonpreemptive}
\end{equation}

\subsubsection{Spatiotemporal Coupling Constraints}
\label{sec:coupling_cons}
The key challenge is \textit{bidirectional spatiotemporal coupling} between 
CSS and DES agents, captured by predicates $\mathcal{P}_{\text{sync}}$ that 
synchronize continuous motion with discrete state transitions. For CSS agent 
$i$ serving DES agent $j$ on task $k$:

\begin{equation}
\mathcal{P}_{\text{sync}}(i, j, k): \quad
\begin{cases}
|\mathbf{p}_i(t) - \mathbf{p}_j^{\text{target}}| \leq \epsilon & \text{(spatial proximity)} \\
q_j^d(t) = \text{idle} & \text{(robot availability)} \\
t \in [\tau_j^k - \Delta t, \tau_j^k] & \text{(temporal window)}
\end{cases}
\label{eq:coupling_predicate}
\end{equation}

where $\epsilon$ is positioning tolerance (typically 0.1--0.5\,m), $\Delta t$ 
is the acceptable early-arrival window (typically 1--5\,s), and $\tau_j^k$ is 
the scheduled start time. The complete coupling constraint set is:

\begin{equation}
\mathcal{C}_{\text{system}} = \bigwedge_{(i,j,k):\, z_{ijk}=1} \mathcal{P}_{\text{sync}}(i, j, k)
\label{eq:coupling_constraints}
\end{equation}

where $z_{ijk} \in \{0,1\}$ indicates whether CSS agent $i$ serves DES agent 
$j$ for task $k$.

We adopt \textit{Boolean satisfaction} (hard constraints) rather than STL 
\textit{quantitative robustness semantics}~\cite{melani2025tree}
for two reasons.
%
First, manufacturing systems demand hard feasibility guarantees: an AGV
arriving outside $[\tau_j^k - \Delta t,\, \tau_j^k]$ causes outright task
rejection, not graceful degradation, so optimizing a robustness degree
$\rho(\phi,\mathbf{x})$ that permits ``nearly satisfied'' constraints is
physically inadmissible.
%
Second, Boolean predicates enable the separable DP decomposition central to
HDP (Section~\ref{sec:Chapter_IV}): CSS-DP and DES-DP enforce hard constraints
via indicator functions $\mathbb{1}[\mathcal{P}_{\text{sync}}]$ in their
Bellman equations (Eq.~\ref{eq:css_bellman},~\ref{eq:des_bellman}), whereas
STL robustness would require evaluating $\rho(\phi,\mathbf{x})$ at every DP
state and increase complexity by a factor of $T_{\text{horizon}}$ due to
STL's temporal operators.
%
Implicit robustness is nonetheless provided by the tolerance parameters
$\epsilon$ and $\Delta t$, which function analogously to STL's
$\Diamond_{[0,\Delta t]}\phi$ operator as hard margins; experiments confirm
this suffices under 40\% task-duration uncertainty
(Section~\ref{sec:robustness}).

\subsection{Problem Statement}

The CDHAS scheduling problem is:

\begin{align}
\label{eq:cdhas_problem}
    \min_{\mathbf{c}, \boldsymbol{\tau}, \mathbf{z}} \quad & T_{\text{makespan}} = \max_{j \in [N_d]} \left( \tau_j^{m_j} + d_j^{m_j} \right) \\
    \text{s.t.} \quad & \text{CSS dynamics}~\eqref{eq:css_dynamics}, \eqref{eq:css_constraints} \\
    & \text{DES logic}~\eqref{eq:precedence}, \eqref{eq:nonpreemptive} \\
    & \text{Coupling } \mathcal{C}_{\text{system}} \text{ from}~\eqref{eq:coupling_constraints} \\
    & \text{Assignment: } \sum_{i \in [N_c]} z_{ijk} = 1, \, \forall j \in [N_d], k \in [m_j]
\end{align}

where decision variables are: $\mathbf{c}$ (CSS control
trajectories), $\boldsymbol{\tau}$ (DES task start times), and
$\mathbf{z}$ (task-agent assignments). The objective minimizes
makespan (total completion time). The assignment constraint ensures each task
is served by exactly one CSS agent. Although the makespan expression
involves only the scheduled start times $\tau_j^k$ and processing
durations $d_j^k$ of the robotic arms, it implicitly accounts for AGV
travel times: the coupling constraints require each
assigned AGV to arrive at the designated workstation before the
corresponding task can begin, so a longer AGV travel time forces a
later $\tau_j^k$, which in turn increases the makespan. In this sense,
minimizing makespan simultaneously incentivizes efficient AGV routing
and compact task scheduling---the two objectives are inseparable.

\subsection{Intractability of the Coupled Problem}

\begin{proposition}
The CDHAS scheduling problem~\eqref{eq:cdhas_problem} is NP-hard.
\label{prop:np_hard}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
We prove NP-hardness by polynomial-time reduction from the Job Shop Scheduling 
Problem (JSSP), which is known to be NP-hard~\cite{zheng2024continuous}.

\textbf{Reduction construction:} Given a JSSP instance with $n$ jobs, $m$ 
machines, and processing times $\{p_{ij}\}$, we construct a CDHAS instance 
as follows: (i) Create $n$ CSS agents with trivial dynamics (single-point 
position space, $v_{\max} = \infty$), eliminating continuous optimization. 
(ii) Create $m$ DES agents corresponding to machines, all co-located with 
CSS agents (eliminating spatial constraints). (iii) Create tasks $\{T_j^k\}$ 
corresponding to job operations with durations $d_j^k = p_{ij}$ and precedence 
matching job sequences. (iv) Set coupling constraints trivially satisfied 
since transport is instantaneous.

\textbf{Equivalence:} Any JSSP schedule corresponds to a CDHAS schedule with 
identical makespan. Since CSS dynamics are trivial, only DES scheduling matters, 
and the two problems are equivalent. Conversely, any CDHAS schedule corresponds 
to a JSSP schedule by extracting task start times and machine assignments. 
Optimal solutions have the same makespan: $T_{\text{JSSP}}^* = T_{\text{CDHAS}}^*$.

Since JSSP is NP-hard and the reduction is polynomial-time, the CDHAS scheduling 
problem is NP-hard. \qed
\end{proof}

This complexity result motivates our decomposition-based approach 
(Section~\ref{sec:Chapter_IV}), which achieves near-optimal solutions in 
polynomial time for practical problem sizes by exploiting the separable 
structure of CSS and DES subproblems.

\section{Hybrid Dynamic Programming Framework}
\label{sec:Chapter_IV}

We present the Hybrid Dynamic Programming (HDP) framework for solving the 
CDHAS problem~\eqref{eq:cdhas_problem}. HDP decomposes the intractable joint 
optimization into two coordinated subproblems: Continuous State Space Dynamic 
Programming (CSS-DP) for trajectory optimization and Discrete Event System 
Dynamic Programming (DES-DP) for task scheduling.

\subsection{Framework Overview}

Fig.~\ref{fig:hdp_framework} illustrates the HDP architecture.
As shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:hdp_framework}(A), the physical scenario
comprises three AGVs (CSS agents) and three robotic arms RA1--RA3
(DES agents), where each AGV must be assigned to and travel to a
robotic arm to deliver materials. 
Note that this scenario depicts a \textit{mid-operation} state rather than the system's initial
configuration: in a typical manufacturing setting, the system
starts with all robotic arms idle and all AGVs co-located at a
central staging area (e.g., a warehouse buffer zone). Here we deliberately select a mid-operation
snapshot---where robotic arms are in mixed busy/idle states and AGVs are spatially dispersed---to better illustrate the bidirectional coupling that HDP resolve.

The framework operates through iterative refinement
(Fig.~\ref{fig:hdp_framework}B): DES-DP generates task schedules
$\boldsymbol{\tau}^{(\ell)}$ and assignments $\mathbf{z}^{(\ell)}$,
CSS-DP computes optimal trajectories $\mathbf{u}^{c,(\ell)}$ and
arrival times $\mathbf{t}^{(\ell)}$, and the Coordinator updates
coupling constraints until convergence.
Fig.~\ref{fig:hdp_framework}(C) details the variable exchange
process across iterations: CSS-DP passes arrival times
$\mathbf{t}^{(\ell)}$ to DES-DP, which returns an updated schedule
$\boldsymbol{\tau}^{(\ell+1)}$; the resulting makespan decreases
monotonically until the improvement falls within a defined scope.

\begin{figure}[t]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=0.92\columnwidth]{fig/fig_hdp_architecture_new.pdf}
    \Description{Diagram of the HDP framework: decomposition and coordinator flow.}
    \caption{HDP framework architecture.
        \textbf{(A) Physical scenario}: Three AGVs (CSS agents, circles)
        deliver materials to three robotic arms RA1--RA3 (DES agents,
        rectangles).
        \textbf{(B) Decompose--Coordinate--Converge}: The CDHAS problem
        is decomposed into CSS-DP (trajectory optimization) and DES-DP
        (task scheduling); the Coordinator iteratively exchanges arrival
        times $\mathbf{t}^{(\ell)}$ and schedules
        $\boldsymbol{\tau}^{(\ell+1)}$ until makespan improvement within a defined scope.
        \textbf{(C) Iterative variable exchange}: CSS-DP computes arrival times given the
        current schedule, DES-DP updates the schedule given new arrival
        times, and the resulting makespan decreases monotonically.}
    \label{fig:hdp_framework}
\end{figure}
The decomposition is the key to tractability: direct joint DP over the
coupled CSS--DES state space incurs exponential complexity in both the
number of agents and tasks, rendering it computationally infeasible for
practical problem sizes. HDP breaks this curse through two complementary
reductions---\textit{spatial decomposition} and \textit{temporal decomposition}.
As illustrated in Fig.~\ref{fig:hdp_framework}(C), this iterative
coordination reduces the makespan from 18\,s to 14\,s in the
depicted example, a 22\% improvement achieved within a small number
of coordination iterations.

\subsection{Continuous State Space Dynamic Programming (CSS-DP)}

\subsubsection{Problem Formulation}

Given a task schedule $\{\tau_j^k\}$ and assignments
$\{z_{ijk}\}$ from DES-DP, CSS-DP computes minimum-time
trajectories for each CSS agent $i$ to visit assigned targets
$\{\mathbf{p}_{j_\ell}^{\text{target}}\}_{\ell=1}^{n_i}$ in sequence while satisfying
spatiotemporal constraints~\eqref{eq:css_constraints} and coupling
constraints~\eqref{eq:coupling_constraints}.

Let $\mathcal{T}_i^{\text{assigned}} = \{(j_1, k_1), \ldots, (j_{n_i}, k_{n_i})\}$
denote the ordered sequence of tasks assigned to CSS agent $i$ (where
$n_i = \sum_{j,k} z_{ijk}$). The CSS-DP problem for agent $i$ is:

\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\min_{\mathbf{u}_i^c(\cdot)} \quad & \sum_{\ell=1}^{n_i} t_i^{j_\ell k_\ell} \\
\text{subject to} \quad & \dot{\mathbf{x}}_i^c(t) = [\mathbf{v}_i(t), \mathbf{u}_i^c(t)]^\top, \\
& \|\mathbf{v}_i(t)\| \leq v_{\max}, \; \|\mathbf{u}_i^c(t)\| \leq a_{\max}, \\
& \mathbf{p}_i(t) \in \mathcal{W} \setminus \mathcal{O}, \\
& \|\mathbf{p}_i(t_i^{j_\ell k_\ell}) - \mathbf{p}_{j_\ell}^{\text{target}}\| \leq \epsilon, \\
& t_i^{j_\ell k_\ell} \in [\tau_{j_\ell}^{k_\ell} - \Delta t, \tau_{j_\ell}^{k_\ell}]
\end{aligned}
\label{eq:css_dp_problem}
\end{equation}

where $t_i^{j_\ell k_\ell}$ is the arrival time of CSS agent $i$ at target 
$\mathbf{p}_{j_\ell}^{\text{target}}$ for task $(j_\ell, k_\ell)$.

\subsubsection{Bellman Equation and Discretization}

We discretize the continuous state space using a grid with resolution
$\Delta x$ and time step $\Delta t$. We adopt grid-based discretization
rather than function approximation (e.g., neural networks) for three reasons:
(1)~\textit{Optimality guarantees}---grid-based DP provides deterministic
near-optimality bounds with error $O(\Delta x + \Delta t)$
(Theorem~\ref{thm:near_optimality}), whereas function approximation
introduces unquantifiable errors;
(2)~\textit{Obstacle handling}---non-convex obstacles
(Eq.~\ref{eq:css_constraints}) are handled naturally via state masking,
without the convergence difficulties that discontinuous feasible regions
pose for function approximation;
(3)~\textit{Computational tractability}---the resulting state space of size
$O\!\left((W/\Delta x)^{2} \cdot T_{\max}/\Delta t\right)$ per agent
remains tractable with reachability-based pruning
(Section~\ref{sec:acceleration}).

Define the value function:

\begin{equation}
V_i(\mathbf{x}, k, t) = \min_{\mathbf{u}_i^c} \left\{ \text{cost to complete tasks } k, k+1, \ldots, n_i \text{ from state } \mathbf{x} \text{ at time } t \right\}
\label{eq:css_value_function}
\end{equation}

The Bellman equation is:

\begin{equation}
V_i(\mathbf{x}, k, t) = \min_{\mathbf{u} \in \mathcal{U}} \left\{ c(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{u}, \Delta t) + V_i(f(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{u}, \Delta t), k, t + \Delta t) \right\}
\label{eq:css_bellman}
\end{equation}

where $f(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{u}, \Delta t)$ is the discrete-time state
transition from~\eqref{eq:css_dynamics}, $c(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{u}, \Delta t) = \Delta t$
is the time cost, and $\mathcal{U}$ is the discretized control set satisfying
constraints~\eqref{eq:css_constraints}.

Boundary conditions: $V_i(\mathbf{x}, n_i+1, t) = 0$ (all tasks completed),
and $V_i(\mathbf{x}, k, t) = \infty$ if $\mathbf{x}$ violates constraints
(collision or out of bounds).

Algorithm~\ref{alg:css_dp} solves CSS-DP using backward dynamic programming. 
The algorithm iterates backward in time from the final task to the initial 
state, computing optimal value functions and control policies at each stage.

\begin{algorithm}[t]
	\caption{CSS-DP: Continuous State Space Dynamic Programming}
	\label{alg:css_dp}
	\small
	\begin{algorithmic}[1]
		\Require DES schedule $\boldsymbol{\tau} = \{\tau_j^k\}$, task assignments $\mathbf{z} = \{z_{ijk}\}$
		\Ensure CSS trajectories $\{\mathbf{u}_i^c(t)\}$ and arrival times $\{t_i^{jk}\}$
		\State Initialize value function $V_i(\mathbf{x}, t) \leftarrow \infty$ for all states
		\State Set terminal condition: $V_i(\mathbf{x}, T_{\text{horizon}}) $
		\For{each CSS agent $i \in [N_c]$}
		\State Extract target sequence: $\mathcal{S}_i = \{(j,k): z_{ijk}=1\}$ ordered by $\tau_j^k$
		\For{$t = T_{\text{horizon}}-\Delta t$ \textbf{down to} $0$ \textbf{(backward in time)}} % \Comment{Modified: Added explanation}
		\For{each state $\mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{X}_i^c$}
		\State $V_i(\mathbf{x}, t) \leftarrow \min_{\mathbf{u} \in \mathcal{U}} \left[ c(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{u}, t) \cdot \Delta t + V_i(f(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{u}), t+\Delta t) \right]$
		\State Store optimal control: $\mathbf{u}_i^*(\mathbf{x}, t) \leftarrow \arg\min_{\mathbf{u}} [\cdots]$
		\EndFor
		\EndFor
		\State \textbf{Forward pass:} Simulate trajectory $\mathbf{x}_i^c(t)$ using $\mathbf{u}_i^*(\cdot, \cdot)$ from $\mathbf{x}_i^c(0)$
		\State Extract arrival times: $t_i^{jk} \leftarrow \min\{t: \|\mathbf{p}_i(t) - \mathbf{p}_j^{\text{target}}\| \leq \epsilon\}$ for each $(j,k) \in \mathcal{S}_i$
		\EndFor
		\State \Return $\{\mathbf{u}_i^c(t)\}_{i \in [N_c]}, \{t_i^{jk}\}$
	\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}

\subsubsection{Computational Considerations}

The backward iteration (Line 6 of Algorithm~\ref{alg:css_dp}) is necessary 
because future task requirements constrain earlier decisions---an agent must 
plan trajectories knowing where it needs to be later. The forward pass 
(Line 11 of Algorithm~\ref{alg:css_dp}) then executes the computed policy 
to generate the actual trajectory.

State space size per agent is
\begin{equation*}
    |\mathcal{X}_i| = \left(\frac{W}{\Delta x}\right)^{2} \cdot 
    \frac{T_{\text{horizon}}}{\Delta t},
\end{equation*}
growing quadratically with spatial resolution $W/\Delta x$ and linearly 
with the temporal horizon. This quantity directly governs CSS-DP complexity 
(Proposition~\ref{prop:complexity}), and Section~\ref{sec:acceleration} 
introduces pruning techniques that substantially reduce the effective 
state space in practice.

\subsection{Discrete Event System Dynamic Programming (DES-DP)}

\subsubsection{Problem Formulation}

Given CSS arrival times $\mathbf{t} = \{t_i^{jk}\}$ from CSS-DP---where 
$t_i^{jk}$ denotes the arrival time of CSS agent $i$ at the target location 
of DES agent $j$ for task $T_j^k$---DES-DP 
determines optimal task schedules $\boldsymbol{\tau} = \{\tau_j^k\}$ (start 
times) and assignments $\mathbf{z} = \{z_{ijk}\}$ (binary: whether CSS agent 
$i$ serves DES agent $j$ on task $k$) that minimize makespan while satisfying 
precedence~\eqref{eq:precedence}, non-preemption~\eqref{eq:nonpreemptive}, 
and coupling constraints~\eqref{eq:coupling_predicate}.

For each DES agent $j$, define state $s_j^k$ as the completion time of task 
$T_j^{k-1}$ together with the set of candidate arrival times 
$\{t_i^{jk}\}_{i \in [N_c]}$ for the next task $T_j^k$---these arrival times 
are needed because DES-DP must select the optimal CSS agent assignment $z_{ijk}$ 
at each stage. The DES-DP problem is:

\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\min_{\boldsymbol{\tau}, \mathbf{z}} \quad & T_{\text{makespan}} = \max_{j \in [N_d]} (\tau_j^{m_j} + d_j^{m_j}) \\
\text{subject to} \quad & \tau_j^k + d_j^k \leq \tau_j^{k+1}, \quad \forall j, k \\
& \tau_j^k \geq \max_{i: z_{ijk}=1} t_i^{jk}, \quad \forall j, k \\
& \sum_{i=1}^{N_c} z_{ijk} = 1, \quad \forall j, k
\end{aligned}
\label{eq:des_dp_problem}
\end{equation}

The second constraint ensures tasks start only after the assigned CSS agent 
arrives (coupling constraint). The third constraint ensures each task is 
assigned to exactly one CSS agent.

\subsubsection{Dynamic Programming Formulation}

Define the value function for DES agent $j$:

\begin{equation}
W_j(s_j^k) = \min_{\tau_j^k, z_{ijk}} \left\{ \text{makespan for tasks } k, k+1, \ldots, m_j \text{ given state } s_j^k \right\}
\label{eq:des_value_function}
\end{equation}

The Bellman equation is:

\begin{equation}
W_j(s_j^k) = \min_{i \in [N_c]} \left\{ \max\{s_j^{k-1} + d_j^{k-1}, t_i^{jk}\} + d_j^k + W_j(s_j^{k+1}) \right\}
\label{eq:des_bellman}
\end{equation}

where the minimization over $i$ selects the CSS agent assignment, and the 
$\max$ operation enforces both precedence (task $k$ starts after task $k-1$ 
completes) and coupling (task $k$ starts after CSS agent $i$ arrives).

Boundary condition: $W_j(s_j^{m_j+1}) = 0$ (all tasks completed).

Algorithm~\ref{alg:des_dp} solves DES-DP independently for each DES agent 
and then coordinates across agents to compute global makespan.

\begin{algorithm}[t]
    \caption{DES-DP: Discrete Event System Dynamic Programming}
    \label{alg:des_dp}
    \small
    \begin{algorithmic}[1]
        \Require CSS arrival times $\{t_i^{jk}\}$ for all $i \in [N_c]$,
                 $j \in [N_d]$, $k \in [m_j]$;
                 task durations $\{d_j^k\}$
        \Ensure DES schedule $\boldsymbol{\tau} = \{\tau_j^k\}$,
                assignments $\mathbf{z} = \{z_{ijk}\}$
        \For{each DES agent $j \in [N_d]$}
            \State Initialize value function: $W_j(s_j^{m_j+1}) \leftarrow 0$
            \For{$k = m_j$ \textbf{down to} $1$} \Comment{Backward pass}
                \For{each state $s_j^k \in \mathcal{S}_j$}
                    \State $W_j(s_j^k) \leftarrow \min_{i \in [N_c]}
                           \left[ \max\!\left(s_j^k,\ t_i^{jk}\right)
                           + d_j^k + W_j(s_j^{k+1}) \right]$
                    \State Store optimal assignment:
                           $i_j^{k,*} \leftarrow \arg\min_{i \in [N_c]}
                           \left[ \max\!\left(s_j^k,\ t_i^{jk}\right)
                           + d_j^k + W_j(s_j^{k+1}) \right]$
                \EndFor
            \EndFor
            \State \textbf{Forward pass:} Initialize $\tau_j^0 \leftarrow 0$;
                   compute for $k = 1, \ldots, m_j$:
            \State \quad $\tau_j^k \leftarrow
                   \max\!\left(\tau_j^{k-1} + d_j^{k-1},\
                   t_{i_j^{k,*}}^{jk}\right)$
        \EndFor
        \State Construct assignment matrix:
               $z_{ijk} = 1$ if $i = i_j^{k,*}$, else $z_{ijk} = 0$
        \Return $\boldsymbol{\tau} = \{\tau_j^k\},\quad
                \mathbf{z} = \{z_{ijk}\}$
    \end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}

The computational complexity of DES-DP is $O(N_d \cdot M \cdot N_c)$ where 
$M = \sum_{j=1}^{N_d} m_j$ is the total number of tasks. This is polynomial 
and significantly more efficient than MILP formulations, which have exponential 
complexity $O(2^M)$ in the worst case.

\subsection{Coordination Mechanism}

Algorithm~\ref{alg:hdp_coordination} coordinates CSS-DP and DES-DP through 
iterative refinement. Starting from an initial schedule, the algorithm 
alternates between CSS trajectory optimization and DES task scheduling until 
convergence.

\begin{algorithm}[t]
	\caption{HDP Coordination}
	\label{alg:hdp_coordination}
	\small
	\begin{algorithmic}[1]
		\Require Initial schedule $\boldsymbol{\tau}^{(0)}$, assignments $\mathbf{z}^{(0)}$, threshold $\delta$
		\Ensure Converged solution $(\mathbf{u}^{c,*}, \boldsymbol{\tau}^*, \mathbf{z}^*)$
		\State Initialize iteration counter: $\ell \leftarrow 0$
		\Repeat
		\State $\ell \leftarrow \ell + 1$
		\State Solve CSS-DP: $\{\mathbf{u}_i^{c,(\ell)}\}, \{t_i^{jk,(\ell)}\} \leftarrow \text{CSS-DP}(\boldsymbol{\tau}^{(\ell-1)}, \mathbf{z}^{(\ell-1)})$ \Comment{Algorithm~\ref{alg:css_dp}}
		\State Solve DES-DP: $\boldsymbol{\tau}^{(\ell)}, \mathbf{z}^{(\ell)} \leftarrow \text{DES-DP}(\{t_i^{jk,(\ell)}\})$ \Comment{Algorithm~\ref{alg:des_dp}}
		\State Compute makespan: $T_{\text{makespan}}^{(\ell)} \leftarrow \max_{j \in [N_d]} (\tau_j^{m_j,(\ell)} + d_j^{m_j})$
		\State Compute improvement: $\Delta T^{(\ell)} \leftarrow |T_{\text{makespan}}^{(\ell)} - T_{\text{makespan}}^{(\ell-1)}|$
		\Until{$\Delta T^{(\ell)} < \delta$ or $\ell \geq L_{\max}$}
		\Return $(\mathbf{u}^{c,(\ell)}, \boldsymbol{\tau}^{(\ell)}, \mathbf{z}^{(\ell)})$
	\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}

The coordination operates as follows: CSS-DP computes optimal trajectories 
given the current schedule, producing updated arrival times. DES-DP then 
reschedules tasks based on these arrival times, potentially changing 
assignments and start times. This process repeats until the makespan 
stabilizes.

\subsection{Convergence Guarantee}

We establish convergence of the HDP coordination mechanism under two mild 
assumptions on the smoothness of the CSS and DES mappings.

\begin{assumption}[Lipschitz Continuity of CSS-DP]
The CSS arrival time mapping $\Psi: \boldsymbol{\tau} \mapsto \mathbf{t}$ 
satisfies:
\begin{equation}
\|\Psi(\boldsymbol{\tau}') - \Psi(\boldsymbol{\tau})\| \leq L_{\Psi} \|\boldsymbol{\tau}' - \boldsymbol{\tau}\|
\end{equation}
for some $L_{\Psi} > 0$.
\label{ass:lipschitz_css}
\end{assumption}

\textit{Interpretation and justification.} This assumption states that small 
disturbance in the task schedule $\boldsymbol{\tau}$ produce proportionally 
bounded changes in AGV arrival times $\mathbf{t}$. It holds whenever 
the CSS-DP trajectory optimizer is stable: since AGV dynamics are governed 
by bounded-velocity kinematics and the workspace is compact, the optimal 
arrival time varies continuously with the departure schedule. 
Empirically, $L_{\Psi} \approx 4.5$ (Section~\ref{sec:convergence_validation}).

\begin{assumption}[Lipschitz Continuity of DES-DP]
The DES scheduling mapping $\Phi: \mathbf{t} \mapsto \boldsymbol{\tau}$ 
satisfies:
\begin{equation}
\|\Phi(\mathbf{t}') - \Phi(\mathbf{t})\| \leq L_{\Phi} \|\mathbf{t}' - \mathbf{t}\|
\end{equation}
for some $L_{\Phi} > 0$.
\label{ass:lipschitz_des}
\end{assumption}

\textit{Interpretation and justification.} This assumption states that small 
changes in AGV arrival times produce proportionally bounded changes in the 
task release schedule $\boldsymbol{\tau}$. It holds because DES-DP solves a 
finite-horizon scheduling problem whose optimal value function is piecewise 
linear in the input arrival times; the slope is bounded by the maximum 
task-processing rate. Empirically, $L_{\Phi} \approx 1$ due to the 
schedule-stability property: DES-DP rarely reassigns tasks after the first 
few iterations (Section~\ref{sec:convergence_validation}).

\begin{theorem}[Convergence of HDP]
Under Assumptions~\ref{ass:lipschitz_css} and~\ref{ass:lipschitz_des} below, 
the HDP coordination (Algorithm~\ref{alg:hdp_coordination}) converges 
geometrically to a coordinately optimal solution with rate $\rho < 1$:
\begin{equation}
T_{\text{makespan}}^{(\ell+1)} - T_{\text{makespan}}^* \leq \rho \cdot (T_{\text{makespan}}^{(\ell)} - T_{\text{makespan}}^*)
\label{eq:convergence_rate}
\end{equation}
where $T_{\text{makespan}}^*$ is the fixed-point makespan and $\rho = L_{\Psi} \cdot L_{\Phi} \cdot \alpha_{\text{crit}}$ 
with $L_{\Psi}$, $L_{\Phi}$ being Lipschitz constants and $\alpha_{\text{crit}}$ 
the critical coupling strength.
\label{thm:convergence}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Define the composite mapping $\mathcal{F} = \Phi \circ \Psi$ that maps 
schedules to schedules: $\boldsymbol{\tau}^{(\ell+1)} = \mathcal{F}(\boldsymbol{\tau}^{(\ell)})$. 
By Assumptions~\ref{ass:lipschitz_css} and~\ref{ass:lipschitz_des}:
\begin{equation}
\|\mathcal{F}(\boldsymbol{\tau}') - \mathcal{F}(\boldsymbol{\tau})\| \leq L_{\Psi} \cdot L_{\Phi} \|\boldsymbol{\tau}' - \boldsymbol{\tau}\|
\end{equation}

The makespan is bounded by schedule changes through coupling strength 
$\alpha_{\text{crit}}$, giving contraction factor $\rho = L_{\Psi} \cdot L_{\Phi} \cdot \alpha_{\text{crit}}$. 
For $\rho < 1$, the Banach fixed-point theorem guarantees convergence to a 
unique fixed point $\boldsymbol{\tau}^*$ with geometric rate~\eqref{eq:convergence_rate}.
Unrolling the recurrence yields $T_{\text{makespan}}^{(\ell)} - T_{\text{makespan}}^* 
\leq \rho^{\ell}(T_{\text{makespan}}^{(0)} - T_{\text{makespan}}^*)$,
from which the iteration bound in Corollary~\ref{cor:iteration_bound} follows directly.
\qed
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Iteration Bound]
\label{cor:iteration_bound}
Let $\Delta_0 = T_{\text{makespan}}^{(0)} - T_{\text{makespan}}^*$ denote the 
initial suboptimality and $\epsilon > 0$ be a prescribed tolerance. 
Under the conditions of Theorem~\ref{thm:convergence}, 
the number of coordination iterations $L$ required to satisfy
$T_{\text{makespan}}^{(L)} - T_{\text{makespan}}^* \leq \epsilon$ is bounded by:
\begin{equation}
L \;\leq\; \left\lceil \frac{\log\!\left(\epsilon \,/\, \Delta_0\right)}{\log \rho} \right\rceil
\label{eq:iteration_bound}
\end{equation}
In particular, setting $\epsilon = 0.01\,\Delta_0$ (1\% relative tolerance) gives
$L \leq \lceil {-4.605}/{\log \rho} \rceil$, which decreases monotonically as 
$\rho \to 0$.
\end{corollary}

\textbf{Theoretical vs.\ practical convergence rates.}
The contraction factor satisfies $\rho = L_{\Psi} \cdot L_{\Phi} \cdot \alpha_{\text{crit}}$,
where $L_{\Psi}$, $L_{\Phi}$ are the Lipschitz constants of the CSS-DP and 
DES-DP mappings respectively, and $\alpha_{\text{crit}} \in (0,1)$ is the 
critical coupling strength---the fraction of tasks whose makespan is 
sensitive to arrival-time perturbations.
Worst-case estimates ($L_{\Psi} \approx 4.5$, $L_{\Phi} \approx 1$) 
yield $\rho \approx 4.5\,\alpha_{\text{crit}}$; convergence ($\rho < 1$) 
therefore requires $\alpha_{\text{crit}} < 0.22$, i.e., fewer than 22\% 
of tasks are tightly coupled.
In practice, four structural properties jointly reduce the \emph{effective} 
coupling strength $\alpha_{\text{crit}}^{\text{eff}}$, driving 
$\rho_{\text{eff}} = L_{\Psi} \cdot L_{\Phi} \cdot \alpha_{\text{crit}}^{\text{eff}} 
= 0.41 \pm 0.03$ (Section~\ref{sec:convergence_validation}):
(1)~\textit{sparse coupling}---only 20--30\% of tasks have tight temporal 
constraints, directly bounding $\alpha_{\text{crit}}^{\text{eff}} \leq 0.30$;
(2)~\textit{spatial locality}---CSS agents typically serve nearby DES agents,
reducing trajectory sensitivity and hence $L_{\Psi}$;
(3)~\textit{schedule stability}---DES-DP rarely changes assignments after 
initial iterations, reducing the effective $L_{\Phi}$;
(4)~\textit{warm-start initialization}--- a good initial solution reduces the number of iterations needed to reach convergence tolerance, 
though it does not alter $\rho$ itself.

\textbf{Quantitative explanation of observed iteration counts.}
Equation~\eqref{eq:iteration_bound} directly explains the empirically observed
iteration counts. Setting $\epsilon = 0.01\,\Delta_0$ and substituting
representative values of $\rho$:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*, itemsep=2pt]
    \item \textit{Favorable regime} ($\rho_{\text{eff}} = 0.41$, with warm-start,
          $N_d = 3$): $L \leq \lceil {-4.605}/{\log 0.41} \rceil = \lceil 5.17 \rceil = 6$,
          consistent with the empirically observed \textbf{4--6 iterations}.
    \item \textit{Challenging regime} ($\rho \approx 0.60$, without warm-start
          or $N_d = 6$): $L \leq \lceil {-4.605}/{\log 0.60} \rceil = \lceil 9.01 \rceil = 10$,
          consistent with the empirically observed \textbf{8--10 iterations}.
    \item \textit{Worst-case theoretical} ($\rho = 0.68$): 
          $L \leq \lceil {-4.605}/{\log 0.68} \rceil = \lceil 11.93 \rceil = 12$,
          providing a conservative upper bound.
\end{itemize}
These values are \emph{empirically calibrated} upper bounds: $\rho_{\text{eff}}$
is measured experimentally (Section~\ref{sec:convergence_validation}), while
$\rho \approx 0.60$ is estimated from agent-scalability experiments
(Section~\ref{sec:scalability02}). The bound~\eqref{eq:iteration_bound}
thus serves as a \emph{post-hoc} theoretical justification for the observed
iteration counts rather than an \emph{a priori} guarantee.

\subsection{Acceleration Techniques}
\label{sec:acceleration}

We introduce three techniques that reduce HDP's computational complexity while 
preserving solution quality.

\textbf{(1) Reachability-based state space pruning.} For CSS-DP, we prune 
states unreachable within velocity and acceleration limits. Given current 
state $\mathbf{x}$ at time $t$ and target arrival time $\tau$, we compute 
the reachable set:
\begin{equation}
\mathcal{R}(\mathbf{x}, t, \tau) = \{\mathbf{x}': \exists \mathbf{u}(\cdot) \text{ s.t. } \mathbf{x}(t) = \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}(\tau) = \mathbf{x}', \|\mathbf{u}\| \leq a_{\max}\}
\end{equation}
States outside $\mathcal{R}$ are pruned. This reduces state space by 60\% 
on average (Section~\ref{sec:ablation}).

\textbf{(2) Adaptive grid refinement.} We use coarse grids ($\Delta x = 1.0$m) 
in open space and fine grids ($\Delta x = 0.2$m) near obstacles and targets. 
This reduces grid points by 30\% while maintaining accuracy at critical regions.

\textbf{(3) Warm-start initialization.} We initialize HDP with a greedy 
solution: assign each task to the nearest available CSS agent and schedule 
tasks in earliest-deadline-first order. This provides $\boldsymbol{\tau}^{(0)}$ 
and $\mathbf{z}^{(0)}$ that are typically within 15-20\% of optimal, reducing 
iterations needed for convergence from 8-10 to 4-6 (Section~\ref{sec:convergence_validation}).

\textbf{Implementation note.} All three acceleration techniques are enabled 
by default in all experiments reported in Section~\ref{sec:Chapter_V}, 
corresponding to the \textit{HDP-Full} configuration. Their individual 
contributions are quantified through ablation studies in 
Section~\ref{sec:ablation}.

\subsection{Computational Complexity and Near-Optimality}
\label{sec:complexity_nearopt}

This section characterises the theoretical guarantees of HDP from two
complementary angles: first, the quality of the solution it produces
(near-optimality analysis); second, the computational cost required to obtain
that solution (complexity analysis and grid-resolution trade-off).
\subsubsection{Near-Optimality Analysis}

We analyze the quality of HDP solutions relative to the global optimum.

\begin{theorem}[Near-Optimality of HDP]
\label{eq:near_optimality}
Let $T_{\text{HDP}}$ be the makespan obtained by HDP and $T_{\text{opt}}$
be the global optimal makespan. Then:
\begin{equation}
T_{\text{HDP}} \leq (1 + \delta_{\text{CSS}} + \delta_{\text{DES}}) \cdot T_{\text{opt}}
\end{equation}
where $\delta_{\text{CSS}} = O(\Delta x + \Delta t)$ and $\delta_{\text{DES}} = O(1/N_c)$ are approximation
factors from discretization in CSS-DP and DES-DP respectively.
\label{thm:near_optimality}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Decompose the optimality gap into three sources: (1) CSS discretization error 
bounded by $\delta_{\text{CSS}} = O(\Delta x + \Delta t)$, (2) DES discretization 
error bounded by $\delta_{\text{DES}} = O(1/N_c)$ (more CSS agents reduce 
assignment suboptimality), and (3) coordination error that vanishes as 
$\ell \to \infty$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:convergence}. Combining these bounds 
yields~\eqref{eq:near_optimality}. \qed
\end{proof}

For typical parameters ($\Delta x = 0.5$m, $\Delta t = 0.1$s, $N_c = 3$),
we have $\delta_{\text{CSS}} \approx 0.04$ and $\delta_{\text{DES}} \approx 0.03$,
giving a theoretical bound of 7\%. Experiments (Table~\ref{tab:main_results})
show actual gaps of 1.2-3.8\% against MILP optimal solutions, validating the
tightness of our analysis.

\subsubsection{Computational Complexity}

We analyze the computational complexity of HDP at two levels:
the \textit{worst-case theoretical complexity} of the base algorithms
(Proposition~\ref{prop:complexity}), and the \textit{effective empirical
complexity} achieved when the acceleration techniques of
Section~\ref{sec:acceleration} are applied.

\begin{proposition}[Computational Complexity of HDP]
\label{eq:complexity_hdp}
The worst-case time complexity of HDP is:
\begin{equation}
    O\!\left( L \cdot \left[
        N_c \cdot M \cdot \left(\frac{W}{\Delta x}\right)^{\!2}
        \cdot \frac{T_{\text{horizon}}}{\Delta t}
        \;+\;
        N_d \cdot M \cdot N_c
    \right] \right)
\end{equation}
where $L$ is the number of coordination iterations, $M$ is the total number
of tasks, $N_c$ and $N_d$ are the numbers of CSS and DES agents, $W$ is the
workspace size, and $\Delta x$, $\Delta t$ are discretization parameters.
\label{prop:complexity}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Each coordination iteration involves:
(1)~CSS-DP for $N_c$ agents, each solving DP over
$(W/\Delta x)^2 \cdot (T_{\text{horizon}}/\Delta t)$ states for $M/N_c$
tasks on average, giving
$O\!\left(N_c \cdot M \cdot (W/\Delta x)^2 \cdot T_{\text{horizon}}/\Delta t\right)$;
(2)~DES-DP for $N_d$ agents, each solving DP over $M$ tasks with $N_c$
assignment choices, giving $O(N_d \cdot M \cdot N_c)$. 
Multiplying by $L$ iterations yields~\eqref{eq:complexity_hdp}. \qed
\end{proof}

Equation~\eqref{eq:complexity_hdp} exposes distinct scalability
dimensions with qualitatively different characteristics.

\textbf{Task scalability ($M$).}
For fixed workspace and agent counts, the dominant cost is linear in $M$.
With the three acceleration techniques of Section~\ref{sec:acceleration}, the effective complexity reduces to $O(M^{1.8})$
empirically, enabling HDP to solve 100-task problems in under 2 minutes
(Section~\ref{sec:Chapter_V}). 

\textbf{Agent scalability ($N_c$, $N_d$).}
Scaling with the number of agents presents a qualitatively different
challenge from task scalability. The DES-DP term is linear in $N_d$, but
CSS-DP must account for inter-agent collision avoidance, which introduces
$O(N_c^2)$ pairwise constraints in the worst case. Consequently, the
scalability claims in this paper refer specifically to \textit{task
scalability}; agent scalability under dense collision constraints remains
an open challenge discussed in Section~\ref{sec:future_work}.

\subsubsection{Grid Resolution Trade-off}

The CSS-DP term in~\eqref{eq:complexity_hdp} grows as
$O\!\left((W/\Delta x)^{2}\right)$, a manifestation of the curse of
dimensionality inherent to grid-based DP. This introduces a fundamental
trade-off between computational cost and solution accuracy, both of which
are governed solely by the grid resolution $\Delta x$. We characterize
each direction analytically below.

\textbf{(1) Quadratic sensitivity of computation cost.}
The number of grid states per spatial dimension is $\lfloor W/\Delta x
\rfloor$, so the 2-D state space contains $(W/\Delta x)^2$ cells.
Each Bellman update in CSS-DP visits every cell
exactly once per time step, yielding a per-agent, per-task cost of
$O\!\left((W/\Delta x)^2 \cdot T_{\text{horizon}}/\Delta t\right)$.
Consequently, halving $\Delta x$ multiplies the CSS-DP cost by
$2^2 = 4$, and reducing $\Delta x$ by a factor of $k$ multiplies it by
$k^2$. This quadratic growth is structural and cannot be eliminated by
implementation optimizations alone.

\textbf{(2) Linear reduction of discretization error.}
Grid-based DP approximates the continuous value function
$V_i^*(\mathbf{x}, k, t)$ by its piecewise-constant projection onto the
grid. For a Lipschitz-continuous cost function $c(\cdot)$ with constant
$K_c$, the approximation error at each grid cell is bounded by
$K_c \cdot \Delta x$ (first-order interpolation error). Propagating this
local error through $M/N_c$ task stages via the Bellman recursion yields
a cumulative trajectory error:
\begin{equation}
    \varepsilon_{\text{traj}} \;\leq\; \frac{M}{N_c} \cdot K_c \cdot \Delta x
    \;=\; O(\Delta x),
    \label{eq:disc_error}
\end{equation}
which enters the near-optimality bound of Theorem~\ref{thm:near_optimality}
as the $\Delta x$ component of $\delta_{\text{CSS}} = O(\Delta x + \Delta t)$.
Hence, halving $\Delta x$ halves the trajectory error---but at a $4\times$
increase in computation cost, reflecting strongly diminishing returns.

\textbf{(3) Practical implication and mitigation.}
The two results above jointly define the break-even criterion for
resolution selection: given a positioning tolerance $\varepsilon$
(determined by the task specification), the coarsest admissible grid is
$\Delta x^* = O(\varepsilon \cdot N_c \cdot v_{\max} / (M \cdot K_c))$,
beyond which further refinement yields negligible accuracy gain at
quadratically growing cost. For typical manufacturing tasks
($\varepsilon = 0.3$--$0.5$\,m), this criterion yields
$\Delta x^* \approx 0.5$\,m as the recommended operating point.
Adaptive grid refinement---concentrating resolution only near task
locations where the value function varies rapidly---mitigates the quadratic
growth without sacrificing accuracy at critical regions.

\section{Experimental Evaluation}
\label{sec:Chapter_V}
We evaluate HDP across three dimensions: 
(1) solution quality—comparing against baselines and ablating individual components; 
(2) computational behavior—analyzing convergence, task/agent scalability, and grid resolution sensitivity; 
and (3) robustness under task duration uncertainty and diverse workspace layouts. 
All experiments use Python~3.12.10 with NumPy on an Intel Core i7-10700K CPU (8 cores, 3.8 GHz) with 32 GB RAM.

\subsection{Experimental Setup}

\subsubsection{System Configuration}

We consider an AGV-Robotic Arm manufacturing system in a rectangular workspace:

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*, itemsep=3pt]
    \item \textbf{CSS agents (AGVs):} $N_c = 3$ mobile robots with $v_{\max} = 1$ m/s, 
    $a_{\max} = 0.5$ m/s², $d_{\text{safe}} = 0.5$ m, dimensions $0.3 \times 0.3$ m.
    
    \item \textbf{DES agents (Robotic Arms):} $N_d = 3$ stationary manipulators 
    at fixed positions. Each processes one task at a time with durations 
    $d_j^k \sim \mathcal{U}(3, 15)$ s.
    
    \item \textbf{Workspace:} $7 \times 6$ grid (7 m × 6 m) with 4 static 
    obstacles ($1 \times 1$ m each). Grid resolution $\Delta x = 0.5$ m, 
    time step $\Delta t = 0.1$ s.
    
    \item \textbf{Tasks:} Three datasets:
    \begin{itemize}[itemsep=1pt]
        \item \textbf{DS1 (Small):} 4 tasks/robot ($M = 12$ total)
        \item \textbf{DS2 (Medium):} 10 tasks/robot ($M = 30$ total)
        \item \textbf{DS3 (Large):} 20 tasks/robot ($M = 60$ total)
    \end{itemize}
    Each dataset has 10 random instances with different task durations, 
    obstacle placements, and initial AGV positions.
\end{itemize}

This configuration is designed to be both industrially representative and 
experimentally rigorous, motivated by three considerations.

\textbf{Typicality of the base configuration.}
The agent counts $N_c = N_d = 3$ reflect a standard flexible manufacturing cell setup: the AGV scheduling literature consistently uses 2--5 AGVs as a representative senario~\cite{fragapane2021planning, zhong2020multi}. 
The $7 \times 6$ m workspace (42 m²) corresponds to the footprint of a standard industrial robot workstation, consistent with the spatial specifications for robot work cells defined in ISO~10218:2025~\cite{iso10218-2-2025}. 
All kinematic parameters (AGV velocity 1 m/s, task durations 3--15 s, positioning tolerance 0.1--0.5 m) are calibrated from industrial AGV specifications (MiR100, KUKA KMR iiwa) and real manufacturing scenarios.

\textbf{Task scale and dataset construction.}
The task range of $M = 12$--$60$ corresponds to the typical workload of a single production shift in job-shop and flexible manufacturing environments, 
representing a small-to-medium scale in the scheduling literature~\cite{rema2025task}. 
Unlike domains with established benchmarks, the TAMP and heterogeneous-agent scheduling literature---including methods such as PDDLStream, LGP, and Asymov---relies on custom, scenario-specific instances due to the absence of a unified public benchmark~\cite{garrett2021integrated}. 
We therefore construct our datasets from calibrated industrial specifications to ensure physical validity and reproducibility.

\textbf{Coverage through scalability analysis.}
While the base configuration is intentionally small-scale to enable controlled comparison with all baselines, Section~\ref{sec:scalability} systematically evaluates task scalability and agent scalability.

\subsubsection{Baseline Methods}

As discussed in Section~\ref{sec:Chapter_II},
CDHAS intersects with the Task and Motion Planning (TAMP) problem family.
However, existing TAMP solvers (e.g., PDDLStream,
LGP, Asymov) are not directly applicable as
baselines for CDHAS, for two structural reasons.

\textbf{(1) Architectural mismatch in optimization objective.}
Existing TAMP solvers are architected for \textit{feasibility-driven} planning:
they enumerate symbolic action sequences and verify geometric realizability
via per-action motion feasibility checks. This architecture is well-suited
for manipulation tasks where the goal is to find \emph{any} valid plan.
CDHAS, by contrast, demands \textit{optimality-driven} planning in which
AGV arrival times are continuous optimization variables that directly
determine makespan.
Adapting existing TAMP solvers to this objective would require enumeration
over an $O(2^M)$ symbolic search space ($M$ tasks), which is computationally
intractable at the scales we consider.

\textbf{(2) Empirical scalability barrier.} TAMP solvers face combinatorial explosion in the joint task-assignment search space, 
further compounded in CDHAS by the need to re-evaluate continuous trajectories for each candidate discrete plan ~\cite{zhao2024survey}. 
Our preliminary experiments on DS1 confirmed this scalability barrier: PDDLStream returned no solution within 1 hour, 
consistent with the known combinatorial scalability limitations of PDDLStream~\cite{garrett2020pddlstream}.


\textbf{Alternative validation strategy.} This baseline set therefore provides meaningful performance benchmarks
across optimization paradigms, we validate HDP against four baselines that 
collectively cover the full spectrum of optimization paradigms---exact, 
heuristic, receding-horizon, and learning-based:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*, itemsep=3pt]
    \item \textbf{MILP:}~\cite{wang2024more} Monolithic optimization using Gurobi. 
    Serves as a near-optimal benchmark for DS1 only (does not scale to DS2/DS3 
    within 1 hour), establishing a solution quality upper bound.

    \item \textbf{Greedy-Single:} Improved greedy method that jointly considers 
    assignment and trajectory cost. For each task, evaluates all AGV--task pairs 
    and selects the minimum estimated completion time.

    \item \textbf{RHC:}~\cite{yan2021rnn} Receding horizon control with a 10\,s horizon, 
    re-planning every 2\,s. Represents state-of-the-art 
    continuous trajectory optimization with online re-planning.

    \item \textbf{RL (DQN):}~\cite{li2022improved} Deep Q-network trained for 50,000 episodes on 
    random instances. Represents learning-based approaches 
    that have shown promise in multi-agent coordination.
\end{enumerate}
This baseline set provides meaningful performance benchmarks across 
optimization paradigms for CDHAS scheduling. Furthermore, integrating HDP 
within TAMP frameworks represents a promising future direction (Section~\ref{sec:future_work}).


\subsubsection{Evaluation Metrics}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*, itemsep=3pt]

    \item \textbf{Makespan} (primary objective, total completion time):
    \begin{equation}
        T_{\text{makespan}} = \max_{j \in [N_d]} \bigl(\tau_j^{m_j} + d_j^{m_j}\bigr)
    \end{equation}
    where $m_j$ indexes the last task of DES agent $j$, and $\tau_j^{m_j}$,
    $d_j^{m_j}$ are its scheduled start time and processing duration.

    \item \textbf{AGV utilization} (fraction of time AGVs spend actively
    transporting, averaged over all $N_c$ agents):
    \begin{equation}
        \text{Utilization} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N_c} t_i^{\text{travel}}}{N_c \cdot T_{\text{makespan}}} \times 100\%
    \end{equation}
    where $t_i^{\text{travel}}$ is the cumulative travel time of AGV $i$.

    \item \textbf{Computation time:} Wall-clock time to compute a feasible
    solution (seconds).

    \item \textbf{Solution quality gap} (relative deviation from the best
    known makespan $T_{\text{best}}$, i.e., MILP for DS1 and best heuristic
    for DS2/DS3):
    \begin{equation}
        \text{Gap} = \frac{T_{\text{method}} - T_{\text{best}}}{T_{\text{best}}} \times 100\%
    \end{equation}

\end{itemize}

Results are averaged over 10 instances per dataset with 95\% confidence
intervals. Statistical significance uses paired $t$-tests:
$^{***}$\,$p < 0.001$, $^{**}$\,$p < 0.01$, $^{*}$\,$p < 0.05$.

\subsection{Convergence Analysis}
\label{sec:convergence_validation}

Fig.~\ref{fig:convergence} shows solution quality versus cumulative 
computation time for all methods on DS2 (30 tasks). HDP converges 
in 6 CSS--DES coordination rounds totaling 9.8\,s, achieving a 
makespan of 86.3\,s---within 0.9\% of MILP's last incumbent while 
requiring $370\times$ less computation time. RHC reaches a worse 
makespan (95.8\,s) only after 38.4\,s, and MILP exhausts its 
3{,}600\,s budget without certifying optimality.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.7\columnwidth]{fig/fig_convergence_time_axis.pdf}
\Description{Convergence plot for HDP showing makespan over iterations (time axis).}
\caption{Solution quality vs.\ cumulative computation time on DS2
(30 tasks, log-scale time axis).
HDP converges in 6 coordination rounds (9.8\,s) to a makespan of
86.3\,s, consistent with geometric decay at $\rho_{\text{eff}}\approx 0.40$
(Theorem~\ref{thm:convergence}).
MILP's data points represent Branch-and-Bound incumbent updates
(intermediate feasible solutions \emph{without} optimality guarantees);
MILP times out at 3{,}600\,s before certifying optimality.}
\label{fig:convergence}
\end{figure}

To validate the convergence rate analysis in Theorem~\ref{thm:convergence},
we note that each HDP coordination round takes approximately 1.6\,s,
so the six rounds correspond to cumulative times of 1.6, 3.2, 4.8,
6.4, 8.0, and 9.8\,s in Fig.~\ref{fig:convergence}.
We fit the geometric model $\Delta T^{(\ell)} = \Delta T^{(0)} \cdot 
\rho_{\text{eff}}^{\ell}$ to the per-round improvements:
$\Delta T^{(1)} = 10.3$\,s, $\Delta T^{(2)} = 4.2$\,s,
$\Delta T^{(3)} = 1.7$\,s, $\Delta T^{(4)} = 0.7$\,s,
$\Delta T^{(5)} = 0.3$\,s, $\Delta T^{(6)} = 0.1$\,s.
Least-squares regression yields $\rho_{\text{eff}} = 0.41 \pm 0.03$
(95\% Confidence Interval), confirming geometric convergence. This is \textit{better
than} the theoretical worst-case prediction of 0.45--0.68 from
Theorem~\ref{thm:convergence}, demonstrating that problem structure
leads to faster convergence in practice.

\subsection{Scalability and Sensitivity Analysis}

\subsubsection{Task Scalability Analysis}
\label{sec:scalability}

Fig.~\ref{fig:scalability} shows computation time vs. problem size (4-100 tasks).

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.85\columnwidth]{fig/fig_scalability.pdf}
\Description{Scalability results: makespan vs. number of tasks for different methods.}
\caption{Scalability comparison. HDP exhibits polynomial growth ($O(M^{1.8})$
empirically fitted) \textit{with respect to task volume} while MILP shows 
exponential growth. HDP solves 100-task problems in under 2 minutes. Note: 
Scalability is evaluated with fixed $N_c = 3$ AGVs and $N_d = 3$ robotic arms.}
\label{fig:scalability}
\end{figure}

\textbf{Task scalability.} HDP's computation time grows as $O(M^{1.8})$ 
(empirically fitted), significantly better than MILP's exponential $O(2^M)$. 
MILP times out for $M > 20$ tasks (1 hour limit), while HDP solves 100-task 
instances in $\approx$ 120 seconds. Greedy-Single remains fastest ($<$ 10 s) 
but sacrifices 15-20\% quality. The empirical exponent 1.8 is slightly better 
than the theoretical $O(M^2)$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:complexity}) due to 
state space pruning becoming more effective for larger problems 
(Section~\ref{sec:acceleration}).

Interestingly, HDP becomes faster than Greedy-Single beyond 70 tasks. This crossover occurs because Greedy-Single's iterative assignment
grows linearly with $M$, while HDP's state space pruning becomes more effective
for larger problems. For $M = 100$, pruning reduces state space by 70-80\%
(vs. 60\% for $M = 30$) due to tighter temporal constraints and spatial
clustering. DP computation cost is amortized over multiple tasks, yielding
effective complexity $O(M^{1.8}/M) = O(M^{0.8})$ per task, while
Greedy-Single evaluates $O(N_c \cdot M)$ candidates sequentially.

\subsubsection{Agent Scalability Analysis}
\label{sec:scalability02}
\textbf{Agent scalability.} While HDP demonstrates strong 
\textit{task scalability} ($O(M^{1.8})$), scaling with respect to the 
number of agents presents different challenges:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*, itemsep=2pt]
    \item \textit{CSS agents ($N_c$)}: Collision avoidance constraints grow 
    as $O(N_c^2)$ (Eq.~\ref{eq:css_constraints}), increasing CSS-DP complexity 
    from $O(N_c \cdot M)$ to $O(N_c^2 \cdot M)$ when collision checking is 
    performed pairwise. Our experiments (Table~\ref{tab:agent_scalability}) 
    show that HDP scales to $N_c = 5$ AGVs within reasonable time ($<$ 5 minutes 
    for 30 tasks), but beyond $N_c = 8$, decentralized variants (e.g., consensus 
    ADMM) may be necessary (Section~\ref{sec:future_work}).
    
    \item \textit{DES agents ($N_d$)}: DES-DP complexity is $O(N_d \cdot M \cdot N_c)$ 
    (Proposition~\ref{prop:complexity}), which is linear in $N_d$. However, 
    coordination iterations $L$ may increase with $N_d$ due to more complex 
    coupling patterns. Empirically, $L$ grows from 4-6 iterations ($N_d = 3$) 
    to 8-10 iterations ($N_d = 6$).
\end{itemize}
To quantify agent scalability, we conduct experiments on DS2 (30 tasks) with 
varying agent configurations. Table~\ref{tab:agent_scalability} shows HDP 
maintains 15-20\% makespan advantage across all configurations, but computation 
time grows super-linearly with $N_c$ due to collision avoidance overhead. 
Increasing from $N_c = 3$ to $N_c = 5$ increases computation time by $3.5\times$ 
(9.8s → 34.7s), consistent with the empirically fitted $O(N_c^{1.6})$ scaling reported in Table~\ref{tab:agent_scalability}. In contrast, 
increasing $N_d$ from 3 to 5 only increases time by $1.5\times$, consistent with the mild super-linear $O(N_d^{1.1})$ dependency observed in the joint fit---substantially weaker than the $O(N_c)$ effect.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\caption{Agent Scalability on DS2 (30 tasks, $7 \times 6$ m workspace)}
\label{tab:agent_scalability}
\small
\begin{tabular}{l|cc|cc}
\toprule
\multirow{2}{*}{\textbf{Configuration}} & \multicolumn{2}{c|}{\textbf{Makespan (s)}} & \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{Comp. Time (s)}} \\
& HDP & Greedy & HDP & Greedy \\
\midrule
$N_c=2$, $N_d=3$ & 112.4 & 128.7 & 7.2 & 1.8 \\
$N_c=3$, $N_d=3$ (default) & 87.2 & 103.4 & 9.8 & 2.1 \\
$N_c=4$, $N_d=3$ & 71.3 & 89.6 & 18.5 & 2.5 \\
$N_c=5$, $N_d=3$ & 63.8 & 82.1 & 34.7 & 3.1 \\

\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\textbf{Practical implications.} These results clarify HDP's scalability profile:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*, itemsep=2pt]
    \item \textit{Task scalability} is the primary strength, enabling 
    $M = 4$-100 tasks with polynomial complexity.
    
    \item \textit{Agent scalability} is acceptable for typical manufacturing 
    cells ($N_c, N_d \leq 5$), where agent counts are fixed by factory layout 
    and remain constant~\cite{wang2024smart}.
    
    \item For large-scale systems ($N_c > 8$), hierarchical decomposition 
    (partition workspace into zones) or decentralized coordination (consensus 
    ADMM) is recommended to break the $O(N_c^2)$ barrier 
    (Section~\ref{sec:future_work}).
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Grid Resolution Sensitivity Analysis}
\label{sec:grid_sensitivity}

\begin{figure}[htpb]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.85\columnwidth]{fig/fig_grid_sensitivity.pdf}
\Description{Grid resolution sensitivity: computation time and makespan vs. grid size.}
\caption{Grid resolution sensitivity on DS2 (30 tasks). \textbf{Left}: 
Computation time grows quadratically with finer grids (exponent 1.97). 
\textbf{Right}: Makespan improves with finer resolution but plateaus 
at $\Delta x \approx 0.3$ m. The optimal choice is $\Delta x = 0.5$ m 
(red marker), balancing accuracy (3.2\% error) and speed (9.8 s).}
\label{fig:grid_sensitivity}
\end{figure}

Fig.~\ref{fig:grid_sensitivity} shows the trade-off between grid resolution 
$\Delta x$ and computation time/solution quality on DS2 (30 tasks).

\textbf{Quadratic computational sensitivity.} Computation time grows as 
$O((W/\Delta x)^2)$: refining from $\Delta x = 0.5$m to 0.25m increases 
CSS-DP time from 9.8s to 39s ($4\times$), while refining to 0.1m increases 
to 245s ($25\times$). 

\textbf{Diminishing returns on accuracy.} Makespan improvement shows diminishing 
returns: $\Delta x = 0.5$m achieves 87.2s, $\Delta x = 0.2$m improves to 86.1s 
(1.3\% gain), while $\Delta x = 0.1$m only improves to 85.8s (0.3\% additional 
gain) at $25\times$ computational cost.

\textbf{Practical recommendation:} For typical manufacturing tasks 
($\epsilon = 0.3$--$0.5$\,m), $\Delta x = 0.5$ m provides the best balance 
(3-4\% discretization error, $<$ 10 s computation for 30 tasks). High-precision 
applications ($\epsilon < 0.2$m) should use adaptive discretization.

\textbf{Practical guideline:} For manufacturing applications, we recommend:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*, itemsep=2pt]
    \item \textit{Standard tasks} ($\epsilon = 0.3$-0.5 m): $\Delta x = 0.5$ m 
    (3-4\% error, $<$ 10 s for 30 tasks)
    \item \textit{High-precision tasks} ($\epsilon = 0.1$-0.2 m): $\Delta x = 0.25$ m 
    with adaptive discretization (1-2\% error, $<$ 20 s for 30 tasks)
    \item \textit{Large workspaces} ($W > 20$ m): Workspace partitioning 
    (Section~\ref{sec:future_work}) to maintain $\Delta x = 0.5$ m locally
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Robustness Analysis}
\label{sec:robustness}
We evaluate HDP's robustness under two sources of real-world variability:
(1) uncertain task durations and (2) diverse workspace layouts.

\subsubsection{Robustness to Task Duration Uncertainty}

Real-world manufacturing tasks have uncertain durations due to variations in 
material properties, robot performance, or environmental conditions. We 
introduce Gaussian noise to task durations:
\begin{equation}
d_j^{k,\text{actual}} = d_j^{k,\text{nominal}} \cdot (1 + \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2))
\end{equation}
where $\sigma \in \{0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4\}$ represents 10-40\% uncertainty.

Fig.~\ref{fig:robustness_duration} shows makespan degradation under increasing 
uncertainty. HDP maintains 12-19\% improvement over Greedy-Single even under 
40\% uncertainty, demonstrating robust performance.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.85\columnwidth]{fig/fig_robustness.pdf}
\Description{Robustness evaluation plots across disturbance levels and layouts.}
\caption{Robustness to task duration uncertainty. HDP's advantage over 
Greedy-Single persists across all uncertainty levels, with graceful degradation 
as uncertainty increases.}
\label{fig:robustness_duration}
\end{figure}

\subsubsection{Robustness to Workspace Layout}

We test HDP on three layout variants to evaluate generalization:

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*, itemsep=2pt]
    \item \textbf{Layout A (Sparse):} 2 obstacles, open workspace
    \item \textbf{Layout B (Standard):} 4 obstacles (default)
    \item \textbf{Layout C (Dense):} 8 obstacles, narrow corridors
\end{itemize}

Table~\ref{tab:robustness_layout} shows HDP maintains consistent performance 
across layouts, with makespan increasing only 8-12\% in dense layout due to 
longer collision-free paths. HDP's advantage actually increases in dense 
layouts (19.9\% vs. 15.5\% in sparse), suggesting coupling-aware optimization 
becomes more valuable when navigation constraints are tighter.

\subsection{Summary}

Taken together, these results confirm that HDP bridges the gap between
theoretical optimality and practical deployability: it achieves near-optimal
makespan with polynomial complexity, remains robust under real-world
uncertainties, and its empirical convergence behavior closely tracks
theoretical predictions.

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:Chapter_VI}

We addressed the CDHAS scheduling problem in intelligent manufacturing,
where bidirectional spatiotemporal coupling between AGV trajectories and
robotic arm task assignments creates a circular dependency that traditional
sequential methods cannot resolve.

\subsection{Summary of Contributions}
\label{sec:contributions}
We proposed the Hybrid Dynamic Programming (HDP) framework via a
decompose-coordinate-converge strategy. Theoretically, we proved that the
NP-hard coupled problem decomposes into tractable CSS-DP and DES-DP
subproblems under mild separability conditions, with geometric convergence
guarantees ($\rho = L_{\Psi} \cdot L_{\Phi} \cdot \alpha_{\text{crit}} < 1$)
and polynomial task scalability $O(M^{1.8})$
(Sections~\ref{sec:Chapter_III}--\ref{sec:Chapter_IV}). Practically, three
acceleration techniques---reachability-based pruning, adaptive discretization,
and warm-start initialization---reduce CSS state space by 60--80\%, enabling
HDP to scale to problem sizes where MILP times out. Empirically, HDP achieves
near-optimal solution quality and significant makespan reduction with robust
performance under uncertainty, confirming that coupling-aware joint
optimization outperforms sequential baselines
(Section~\ref{sec:Chapter_V}).

\subsection{Limitations and Future Directions}
\label{sec:future_work}

\textbf{(1) Grid resolution sensitivity.}
Grid-based CSS-DP exhibits quadratic computational sensitivity
$O((W/\Delta x)^2)$ and approximately 3\% discretization error at
$\Delta x = 0.5$\,m, which becomes prohibitive for high-precision applications
($\epsilon < 0.1$\,m). Future work will pursue adaptive discretization
(dynamically adjusting grid resolution based on local obstacle density) and
hybrid planning (combining grid-based DP for global routing).



\textbf{(2) Agent scalability and TAMP integration.}
Scaling with CSS agents is constrained by quadratic collision avoidance
complexity $O(N^2)$. Two directions are planned: decentralized coordination via consensus
ADMM, where each CSS agent optimizes its own trajectory while exchanging only
local coupling variables, and hierarchical decomposition that partitions large
fleets into smaller teams coordinated by a higher-level scheduler.
More broadly, embedding CSS-DP as a numeric trajectory optimization module
within TAMP frameworks (e.g., PDDLStream) is a promising direction, where HDP's optimality guarantees and bidirectional
coupling resolution complement symbolic high-level reasoning.


\textbf{(3) Static environment assumptions.}
The current formulation assumes static obstacles and known task durations.
Although HDP maintains performance under uncertainty (up to 40\%, Section~\ref{sec:robustness}), fully dynamic
environments with online task arrivals and moving obstacles remain an open
challenge. Rolling horizon optimization with warm-start re-planning provides
a near-term direction, while robust DP formulations and predictive obstacle
avoidance offer a longer-term direction.
